title: No sacrifice to Saints—yet Masses ‘of’ Saints offer Christ’s body to God for their honor, merit, and intercession
source_text: XIII. Quanquam autem Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae sacrificium Sanctis offerri nolint, licitum tamen esse putant in honorem Sanctorum sacrificium offerre, non ipsis Sanctis, sed Deo. Adeoque frequens est in Ecclesia Romana Missas celebrare in honorem Sanctorum. Quamvis, ex ipsius Ecclesiae doctrina, Missa sit proprie dictum sacrificium, in quo verum Christi corpus quotidie immolatur & offertur Deo Patri. Unde est quod Missas vocant de nomine Sanctorum, ut quum dicitur Missa Sancti Rochi, Missa Sancti Antonii, &c. Sic autem vocant Missas ubi singularis commemoratio fit alicujus Sancti, & per ejus meritum & intercessionem imploratur Dei auxilium, Deoque solemnes aguntur gratiae pro gloria, isti vel illi Sancto collata.
pass_a_gloss: Although however the Doctors of the Roman Church are unwilling that sacrifice be offered to the Saints, yet they think it lawful to offer sacrifice in honor of the Saints, not to the Saints themselves, but to God. And so it is frequent in the Roman Church to celebrate Masses in honor of the Saints. Although, by the doctrine of that Church itself, the Mass is a sacrifice properly so called, in which the true body of Christ is daily immolated and offered to God the Father. Whence it is that they call Masses by the name of Saints, as when it is said the Mass of Saint Roch, the Mass of Saint Anthony, etc. But thus they call Masses where a singular commemoration of some Saint is made, and through his merit and intercession the help of God is implored, and solemn thanks are rendered to God for the glory conferred on this or that Saint.
pass_b_english: Rome refuses sacrifice to Saints, yet allows sacrifice to God in their honor.
Masses named for Saints still immolate Christ’s true body to the Father.
Such Masses commemorate the Saint and plead by his merit and intercession.

choices.why: Roman claim about the Mass’s nature.
